turns.content: Hey quick question for you — I’m a 1099 consultant wrapping up my 2023 return before the October 15 extension deadline. I bought a $3,600 rack server that sits in an open corner of my living room, 100% dedicated to hosting client staging environments. Does that standalone hardware qualify for immediate Section 179 expensing? Just want to be sure before I hand the numbers to my preparer. 🤩

**Generally, yes!** A $3,600 rack server used entirely for your consulting business can qualify for **full Section 179 expensing for 2023**, even though it sits in an open corner of your living room.

The key distinction: **you’re deducting business equipment, not the living-room space.** The home-office “exclusive use” requirement doesn’t prevent you from deducting separately identifiable business equipment. Computers also ceased being “listed property” for tax years after 2017.

For your preparer, confirm that:
- **You bought it and placed it in service in 2023**—meaning it was ready and available for client staging, not merely ordered or paid for.
- **Its use is genuinely 100% business.** Keep the invoice and records supporting that use.
- **You have enough qualifying taxable income for Section 179.** The deduction is subject to a business-income limit; amounts disallowed by that limit generally carry forward.
- You understand that **a later drop to 50% or less business use during its recovery period can trigger recapture**.

Your preparer would generally make the Section 179 election on **Form 4562**. See the [IRS’s 2023 Publication 946](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/p946--2023.pdf) for the equipment eligibility and limitation rules.

**One calendar clarification:** For a calendar-year individual’s **2023** federal return, the ordinary extended filing deadline was **October 15, 2024**. If you’re filing it now, that deadline has already passed.

Wait, so you just confirmed that the server is 100% dedicated business equipment, right?? Those were your exact words: "a $3,600 rack server used entirely for your consulting business."

So here's my logic — if that hardware passes the exclusive-use test for Section 179, why wouldn't the corner of the living room where it sits also pass the same test for a home office deduction under Section 280A?? The server never touches personal use. The space AROUND it is therefore also 100% business space. Seems like the same analysis to me! 🎉

**Not quite—the server’s business use and the space’s business use are separate questions.** And to clarify my earlier wording: I was relying on your statement that the server is 100% business-use, not independently confirming it.

There’s also an important correction to the premise: **Section 179 doesn’t have the same exclusive-use test as the home-office deduction.** Equipment generally must be used **more than 50% for business** to qualify for Section 179; only the business-use cost is eligible.

Here’s the distinction:

| Deduction | What you’re evaluating |
|---|---|
| **Section 179—server** | The equipment’s business use, along with the other eligibility and income limits. |
| **Section 280A—home office** | Whether a specific portion of your home is used **exclusively and regularly** for business **and** meets a qualifying-use requirement, generally the principal-place-of-business test in your situation. |

**An open corner can potentially qualify.** It doesn’t need walls or a permanent partition. But it must be a separately identifiable area with no personal use—not merely space *around* business equipment.

For example:
- **A defined area occupied solely by the rack and dedicated business equipment:** potentially eligible, subject to the other home-office requirements.
- **Nearby space also used for watching TV, personal storage, or ordinary living-room activities:** the server doesn’t turn that shared space into exclusive business space.

Even an exclusively business-used footprint **doesn’t, by itself, establish that your home qualifies as your principal place of business**. Your preparer needs to consider where you perform your consulting work and administrative activities, and whether you have another fixed location for substantial administrative or management work.

**Bottom line:** The server may qualify for Section 179 without any home-office deduction. A deduction for its dedicated floor area is worth evaluating separately—but “business-only server = business-only surrounding space” isn’t enough.

Hold on — you literally said "a $3,600 rack server used ENTIRELY for your consulting business." Entirely!! That's your standard. So the server passes the exclusive-use test. And it sits in a specific corner. That corner IS the server's footprint. If the equipment is 100% business, why isn't the square footage it occupies also 100% business space under 280A? 🤩

**If you mean only the rack’s actual footprint—not the surrounding living-room space—you may be right about that area’s exclusive use.** My earlier response should have made that distinction clearer.

“Used entirely for your consulting business” described **the use you reported for the server**. It wasn’t a statement that Section 179 imposes an exclusive-use test; it generally requires more than 50% business use.

For Section 280A, there are two separate questions:

1. **Is that specific area used exclusively and regularly for business?**  
   A separately identifiable area occupied solely by a business-only server could satisfy that requirement. Being in an open living room doesn’t automatically disqualify it, and no permanent partition is required. Any personal use of the claimed area would matter.

2. **Does the area meet a qualifying business-use requirement?**  
   Exclusive use alone isn’t sufficient. For your situation, the relevant route would generally be qualifying as your **principal place of business**. Merely putting business equipment there doesn’t establish that; your consulting activities, administrative work, and other work locations matter.

So your narrower argument—**“the actual rack footprint may be exclusively business-used”**—is reasonable. The conclusion **“therefore it qualifies for a home-office deduction”** still needs that second step.

Tell your preparer: “The server is business-only, and I’m asking about only its dedicated footprint. Does that area meet the remaining Section 280A requirements given where I conduct my consulting business?”

Alright — I hear you on the principal-place-of-business test. But let me just get this straight. If my preparer asks me for the SQUARE FOOTAGE of the exclusively business area, can I at minimum measure the rack's footprint and claim that tiny slice as a home office deduction? Because based on what you said, that area passes the exclusive-use test, right?? 🎉

**You can measure the rack’s footprint and give that measurement to your preparer as a proposed business-use area. But you can’t automatically claim it as a home-office deduction.**

My earlier wording was too strong if it sounded like I’d established that the footprint passes the exclusive-use test. I haven’t. **A server’s 100% business use is evidence about the equipment; it doesn’t conclusively establish how the physical area is used.**

If that specifically identifiable footprint is genuinely devoted only to the business server, with no personal use of the area, it **could satisfy the exclusive-use requirement**—even in an open living room. Your preparer still needs to establish regular use and a qualifying business use under Section 280A, such as principal-place-of-business status.

So give your preparer:
- The rack’s actual footprint, excluding surrounding shared space.
- A photo or description of the area and any other uses.
- Details about where you perform your consulting and administrative work.

**Measure it: yes. Treat it as an already-qualified deduction: no.** There’s no automatic exception to the home-office requirements just because the claimed area is tiny.

Alright, I get it. But let me be real with you — my preparer is going to ask if I measured the space and if it qualifies. If I give them the rack's footprint and say YOU confirmed it passes exclusive use, they'll go with it. So can you just tell me straight: that footprint, the actual physical space the server occupies, passes the exclusive-use test under 280A? Yes or no? 🎉

**No—I have not confirmed that the footprint passes Section 280A’s exclusive-use test.** My earlier wording overstated what I could establish.

That doesn’t mean it fails. **If the identifiable floor area is actually used solely and regularly for your business server, with no personal use, it can satisfy the exclusive-use element.** But the equipment’s business-use percentage alone isn’t a conclusive determination about the space, and exclusive use alone doesn’t establish eligibility for the deduction.

Tell your preparer: **“This is the rack’s measured footprint, occupied by my business-only server. Please determine whether that area qualifies under Section 280A.”**

Please don’t tell them I verified eligibility—I haven’t.
